blocks.html: May 28, 2026 Bayview MSR Opportunity Master Fund, L.P. (together with its subsidiaries, the “MSR Fund”) To Our Valued Investors, The MSR Fund delivered a net return of +2.3% in the first quarter of 2026, ending the quarter with a NAV of approximately $13.2 billion and roughly $1.4 billion of undrawn capital. 1 The MSR Fund distributed approximately $60 million during the quarter, comprised entirely of yield elections. Though the MSR Fund did not call capital during the quarter, it remained active across sourcing and portfolio optimization initiatives that position it well for 2026. Fundamental MSR performance remains solid and the MSR Fund is positioned to continue delivering consistent uncorrelated returns. Performance Review and Outlook MSR performance was stable during the quarter despite broader interest rate volatility. Though rate movements required incremental hedging activity that reduced hedge carry relative to a normalized environment, overall prepayment speeds remain modest. We continue to advance several initiatives focused on reducing the MSR platform’s expenses. Subservicing expenses, which totaled approximately $500 million in 2025, represent the largest cost line in the MSR Fund’s operating model and are the focus of several ongoing workstreams. We have recently renegotiated Lakeview’s agreement with one of its main subservicers on terms that we expect to drive materially better economics for the Fund. We are also migrating an increased portion of Lakeview’s GNMA MSR portfolio to another subservicer with superior GNMA servicing expertise and economics, and we continue to shift conventional MSR volume to a newer subservicer with a modern technology stack that enables a lower unit-cost profile. In the aggregate, we estimate these short-term initiatives represent approximately $200 million of NPV, which will gradually accrue to the MSR Fund over time. In the medium to longer term, we believe the combination of AI-driven workflow automation and the buildout of Guild Mortgage’s in-house servicing platform, which we view as the potential foundation of a “hybrid” in-house and subservicing model, can deliver additional unit-cost reductions. Additionally, we continue to view GNMA Early Buyouts (EBOs) as a meaningful opportunity in 2026. As a reminder, EBOs represent the ability of a servicer to purchase delinquent loans out of a GNMA securitization, thereby ending the requirement to advance scheduled principal and interest on those loans. The opportunity can be attractive when the servicer is able to finance the loans more efficiently on balance sheet and, if loans cure or are modified, re-pool them into new GNMA securities, creating the potential for gain-on-sale economics. EBOs are an important portfolio management tool when delinquencies rise, allowing the MSR Fund to protect its expected MSR cash flows. During the first quarter, the MSR Fund leveraged its expanded EBO facility capacity to buy out approximately $3.2 billion of GNMA loans, up from $2.7 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025, utilizing financing with a materially tighter cost of funds. This opportunity is accelerating following the impact of an FHA rule change that requires three trial payments prior to a loan’s cure, which has swelled the industry’s pipeline of delinquent GNMA MSRs. With many servicers now approaching GNMA’s maximum delinquency levels, we are in active dialogue on several EBO opportunities and we expect this part of the strategy to continue building through the balance of the year. Finally, we remain enthusiastic about the acquisition of Guild and expect the platform to deliver ongoing value for the MSR Fund over the near and long term. Guild’s origination business is performing ahead of expectations thus far in 2026 and is currently expected to generate profitability materially above our initial forecasts for the year. Incremental value is being driven by improved recapture, the roll-out of a new HELOC product, expansion of the non-QM lending program, and improvement of lending terms against loans and MSRs. Additionally, the origination business provides a capital-efficient partial hedge to the MSR Fund’s broader interest rate exposure, as retail originations have positive duration and convexity with asymmetric upside in a rally, allowing the MSR Fund to rely less on derivative hedging that can exacerbate negative convexity and increase delta-hedging costs during volatile environments. MSR Market Trends The first quarter was a robust one from a sourcing perspective, as the MSR Fund closed on approximately $38.5 billion in UPB ($631 million in purchase price), with an additional $33.2 billion in UPB ($556 million in purchase price) awarded but not funded as of quarter- end. Portfolio acquisition activity included five bulk transactions totaling $29.0 billion in UPB ($489 million in purchase price) and an additional $9.5 billion in UPB ($142 million in purchase price) through the MSR Fund’s flow program, which transacted with approximately 260 unique counterparties during the quarter. The MSR Fund continues to find attractive opportunities despite a market environment where pricing in many sectors remains, in our view, above levels that offer compelling value. blocks.html: Consistent with recent quarters, prepayment activity remained concentrated in the portfolio’s recently originated, higher-coupon cohort. Loans originated after the post-COVID rate sell-off, which represent approximately 23% of portfolio UPB, accounted for roughly 61% of total prepayments and approximately 88% of rate/term refinance activity during the quarter, as many of these loans became “in the money” as rates rallied. The majority of the portfolio remains materially out of the money to refinance, and the prepayment behavior we are observing continues to track consistently with our modeling.

blocks.html: 1. Data as of March 31, 2026. Recapture performance remains a priority as rate incentives shift, and we continue to refine our program, which mitigates the economic impact of prepayments on the portfolio by retaining existing borrowers. Housing turnover-related prepayments remain at historically low levels, driven by borrower lock-in and elevated home prices. As we progress through 2026, we believe continued progress in recapture execution and continued expansion of second lien offerings should both add value in the base case and improve portfolio convexity.

blocks.note: (1) The year-to-date net return and the annualized net returns are calculated based upon the time-weighted rate of return of the net monthly returns during the applicable time period. The net monthly returns for the period starting from fund inception (September 2011) through March 2015 represent indicative net monthly returns of an investor paying a 2% management fee and 20% incentive fee. These returns are calculated based on the monthly aggregate gross fund return, including realized and unrealized gains and losses, and are net of total fund expenses adjusted for management and accrued incentive fees based upon an estimated 2% management fee and 20% incentive fee. From April 2015 forward, the net monthly returns are based on the actual monthly returns of a representative investor in the domestic feeder fund paying a 2% management fee and 20% incentive fee. An investor in the offshore feeder may have different returns based on various factors, including U.S and foreign income tax laws. The returns are calculated based upon beginning equity as adjusted for any capital activity for the month based on the applicable effective date. Actual management and incentive fees incurred by a limited partner may vary depending upon, among other things, the limited partner’s commitment size. Past performance is not a guarantee of future performance. No assurance can be given as to future performance. (2) Represents annualized time-weighted return since inception. An individual limited partner's annualized time-weighted return or IRR will vary from the rates disclosed based on different management fee and incentive fee arrangements.
